x: Commentary on Sūrat al-Jinn (The Jinn). In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.
Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted:
h

Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened, and they said: “We have heard a wondrous Qurʾān (1), guiding to right conduct, and we have believed in it. We will never associate anyone with our Lord (2). And exalted is the majesty of our Lord: He has taken neither wife nor child (3).”

God, glorified is His praise, says to His Prophet Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him: Say, Muḥammad: God revealed to me “that a group of jinn listened” to this Qurʾān, “and they said” to their people when they heard it: “We have heard a wondrous Qurʾān
n
, guiding to right conduct”—that is, pointing to the truth and the correct path.

“And we have believed in it”—that is, [we have affirmed it] (1). “We will never associate anyone with our Lord” among His creatures. The reason this group of jinn listened to the Qurʾān is related as follows.

c: Muḥammad b. Muʿammar told me: Abū Hishām al-Makhzūmī related to us: Abū ʿAwānah related to us, from Abū Bishr, from Saʿīd b.
m: Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of God did not recite to the jinn, nor did he see them. The Messenger of God set out with a group of his Companions, heading for the market of ʿUkāẓ. The devils had been prevented from getting news from heaven, and shooting stars had been sent against them. The devils returned to their people, who asked them: What is the matter with you? They said: We have been prevented from receiving news from heaven, and shooting stars have been sent against us. They said: Nothing has come between you and the news of heaven except some new event. He said: Go and search the eastern and western regions of the earth to see what has happened. The group that headed toward Tihāmah set out for the Messenger of God at Nakhlah
n

, while he was on his way to the market of ʿUkāẓ and was leading his Companions in the dawn prayer. When they heard the Qurʾān, they listened to it and said: By God, this is what has come between you and the news of heaven. It was then that they returned to their people and said: “Our people, we have heard a wondrous Qurʾān (1), guiding to right conduct, and we have believed in it. We will never associate anyone with our Lord.” Ibn ʿAbbās said: Then God revealed to His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, “Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened”—that is, He revealed to him the words of the jinn
n

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān, from ʿĀṣim,
m: from Zirr
n

, who said: A group led by Zawbaʿah and his companions came to Mecca to meet the Prophet. They heard the Prophet reciting, then departed. That is what God says: “When We directed a group of jinn toward you to listen to the Qurʾān, when they were present for it, they said: ‘Listen attentively’” [Q 46:29]. He said: There were nine of them, including Zawbaʿah
n

c: I was told by al-Ḥusayn:
m: I heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd related to us: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say concerning “Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened”: This is God’s saying: “When We directed a group of jinn toward you” [Q 46:29]. Heaven had not been guarded during the interval between Jesus and Muḥammad. When God sent Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him, the lowest heaven was guarded and the devils were pelted with shooting stars. Iblīs said: Something has happened on earth. He ordered the jinn to scatter across the earth and bring him news of what had happened. The first group he sent were people from Naṣībīn, a land in Yemen; they were the noblest and foremost of the jinn. He sent them toward Tihāmah and the lands adjoining Yemen. That group set out and came to the valley of Nakhlah, a two-night journey along the valley. There they found the Prophet of God, peace and blessings be upon him, performing the morning prayer. They heard him reciting the Qurʾān: “When they were present for it, they said: ‘Listen attentively.’ When it was finished”—that is, when the prayer was over—“they returned to their people as warners” [Q 46:29]. He says: As believers. The Messenger of God did not know of them or notice that anyone had been directed to him until God revealed to him: “Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened.”

x: His saying, “And exalted is the majesty of our Lord”: The authorities on interpretation differed about its meaning.
Some said that it means: We believed in Him, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord; and we believed that our Lord’s command, authority, and power are exalted. We mention who said this.

c: ʿAlī told me: Abū Ṣāliḥ related to us: Muʿāwiyah related to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning His saying, “And exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He said: His act, command, and power
n

c: Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: My father related to me; my uncle related to me; my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning His saying, “And exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He says: Our Lord’s command is exalted.

c: Muḥammad b. Bashshār and Muḥammad b. al-Muthannā related to us,
m: both saying: Muḥammad b. Jaʿfar related to us: Shuʿbah related to us, from Qatādah, concerning this verse, “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He says: Our Lord’s command
n
b.via: Muḥammad b. Bashshār and Muḥammad b. al-Muthannā

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us
m: n
: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān, from al-Suddī, concerning “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He said: Our Lord’s command
n

c: Yūnus told me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd said
m: concerning His saying, “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord; He has taken neither wife nor child.” He said: His command is exalted above taking—as they claimed—a wife or child. He recited: “Say: He is God, One; God, the Eternal Refuge” [Q 112:1–2] through the end of the sūrah
n
. He said: That could never be the case for Him.

x: Others said that what is meant is the majesty and renown of our Lord. We mention who said this.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us: al-Muʿtamir b. Sulaymān related to us, from his father, who said: ʿIkrimah said
m: concerning God’s saying, “the majesty of our Lord”: The majesty of our Lord
n

c: Muḥammad b. ʿUmārah told me: Khālid b. Yazīd related to me: Abū Isrāʾīl related to us, from Fuḍayl, from Mujāhid,
m: concerning His saying, “And exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He said: The majesty of our Lord
n

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān, from Sulaymān al-Taymī, who said:
m: ʿIkrimah said, “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord”: The majesty of our Lord
n

c: Bishr related to us: Yazīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah,
m: concerning His saying, “And exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He said: His majesty, greatness, and command are exalted.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah,
m: concerning “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He said: Our Lord’s command is exalted; His greatness is exalted
n

x: Others said that what is meant is
n
: Our Lord’s wealth. We mention who said this.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us: al-Muʿtamir b. Sulaymān related to us, from his father, who said: al-Ḥasan said
m: concerning His saying, “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord”: The wealth of our Lord
n

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān, from Sulaymān al-Taymī, from al-Ḥasan,
m: concerning “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He said: The wealth of our Lord
n

c: Yaʿqūb b. Ibrāhīm told me: Ibn ʿUlayyah related to us, from Abū Rajāʾ, from al-Ḥasan,
m: concerning His saying, “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He said: The wealth of our Lord
n

c: Al-Ḥasan b. ʿArafah related to us: Hushaym related to us, from Sulaymān al-Taymī, from al-Ḥasan and ʿIkrimah,
m: concerning it. One of them said: His wealth; the other said: His greatness.

x: Others said that what was meant was “grandfather,” the father’s father. They said that this was [an ignorant expression used by the jinn]
n
. We mention who said this.

c: Abū al-Sāʾib told me: Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Sārah related to me, from his father, from Abū Jaʿfar,
m: concerning “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He said: This was an expression
n
used by ignorant jinn
n

x: Others said that what was meant was His renown. We mention who said this.

m: Muḥammad b. ʿAmr told me: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us: ʿĪsā related to us.

c: Al-Ḥārith also told me: al-Ḥasan related to us: Warqāʾ related to us,
m: both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, concerning God’s saying, “Exalted is the majesty of our Lord.” He said: His renown
n

. In our view, the soundest interpretation is that it means: The greatness, power, authority, and might of our Lord are exalted. We said this is the soundest interpretation because the word jadd has two meanings in Arabic. One is “grandfather,” the father’s father or mother’s father
n

. It is not permissible to describe God in this way in the case of these jinn whom God described, since they said: “We have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.” Whoever describes God as having a father
n
or grandfather
n

—the father’s father or mother’s father—there is no doubt that he is among the associators. The other meaning of jadd is “fortune” or “share”; one says that a man has jadd in a matter when he has a share in it. In Persian this is called bakht, “good fortune.” This is the meaning intended by the group of jinn when they said, “And exalted is the majesty of our Lord,” God willing: His share of dominion, authority, power, and greatness is exalted. He therefore has neither wife nor child, because a wife is only taken by someone weak and incapable, compelled by the desire that urges him to take one
n
; and a child only comes from a desire that urges him to sexual intercourse
n

, from which a child results. The group of jinn thus said: The dominion, authority, power, and greatness of our Lord are far above weakness like that of His creatures, whom desire compels to take a wife or have intercourse that results in a child. God’s report about them confirms the soundness of what we have said: [He reports that they said, “He has taken neither wife nor child,” and so He informed us]
n

that they declared God far above taking a wife or child when they said: “And exalted is the majesty of our Lord; He has taken neither wife nor child.” In this sense, one says rajulun jaddiyy, jadīd, or majdūd, meaning a man fortunate in what he has; from this comes the verse of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī
n
: “Go forth, Banū Thaʿl, for war is your fortune; count the water-skins
n
, and do not weep for the one slain”
n
. Another poet said
n

: “May your fortune rise! I am a man whom enemies have driven to you in successive waves.” His saying, “He has taken no wife” means a spouse, “nor child.” The readers differed in how they read His saying, “And that the majesty of our Lord is exalted.” Abū Jaʿfar the reader read this and six other passages with a fatḥah, including “that a group of jinn listened,” “the mosques belong to God,” “our fool used to say,” “men among humankind used to,” and “when God’s servant stood up calling upon Him,” as well as “if they had remained straight on the path”
n
. Nāfiʿ read all of them with a kasrah
n
, except for three: “Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened”; “if they had remained straight on the path”; and “the mosques belong to God”
n

. As for the readers of Kūfah other than ʿĀṣim, they read all the passages at the end of Sūrat al-Najm and the beginning of Sūrat al-Jinn with a fatḥah, except for “then they said: ‘We have heard’” and “He said: ‘I only call upon my Lord’”
n

, and what follows it through the end of the sūrah, which they read with a kasrah, except for “so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord.” As for ʿĀṣim, he read all of them with a kasrah except “the mosques belong to God,” which he read with a fatḥah
n
. Abū ʿAmr read all of them with a kasrah [from the beginning] through “if they had remained straight on the path”; he read that and what follows it with a fatḥah
n

. Those who read nearly all of them with a fatḥah, except where they occur as quotations—such as “then they said: ‘We have heard’” or “He said: ‘I only call upon my Lord’”—connected every “that” in the sūrah to His saying, “and we believed in it,” meaning that they believed in all of it. They therefore read them with a fatḥah because they are governed by “believed.” Al-Farrāʾ said
n

: Do not let it prevent you from finding that “believed” sounds awkward with a fatḥah in some of these cases; where expressing “believed” explicitly is awkward, another verb parallel to believing may be understood, requiring “that” to be read with a fatḥah. The Arabs said
n

: “When the beautiful women appear one day, and they line their eyebrows and their eyes,” where “their eyes” is accusative by association with “their eyebrows,” although eyes are not lined but darkened with kohl. The verb “apply kohl” is understood; likewise, where “we believed” does not fit, one can understand “we affirmed,” “we were inspired,” or “we witnessed”
n

. He said: The accusative reading is also supported by His saying, “if they had remained straight on the path.” Whoever reads the previous “that” with a kasrah should omit “that” after “if,” because when “inna” is lightened it is not used in reported speech; one says: “I say, if you had done it, I would have done it,” without adding “that.” As for those who read all of them with a kasrah while reading “if they had remained straight” with a fatḥah, it is as if they understood an oath with “if” and disconnected the phrase from the sequence of the opening words, as if saying: “By God, if only they had remained straight.” The Arabs insert “that” in this position with an oath, and also omit it. A poet said
n
: “I swear, if anyone but you had brought us his message, we would have found no defense for you.” [He said: Another poet recited to me]
n

: “Indeed, by God, if you were free-born—though you are neither free nor noble.” He inserted “that.” Whoever reads all of them with a kasrah but reads “the mosques belong to God” with a fatḥah singles that passage out as revelation
n

; he understands the oath to be implicit in “if they had remained.” As for Nāfiʿ, he read the passages with a fatḥah by connecting them to His saying, “It was revealed to me”; those he read with a kasrah he treated as the words of the jinn. The reading I prefer is a fatḥah where the passage is revelation and a kasrah where it is the words of the jinn, because this is the most eloquent Arabic and clearest in meaning, even though the other readings have defensible grounds.

Abū Jaʿfar the reader read this and six other passages with a fatḥah, including “that a group of jinn listened,” “the mosques belong to God,” “our fool used to say,” “men among humankind used to,” and “when God’s servant stood up calling upon Him,” as well as “if they had remained straight on the path” (6).

As for the readers of Kūfah other than ʿĀṣim, they read all the passages at the end of Sūrat al-Najm and the beginning of Sūrat al-Jinn with a fatḥah, except for “then they said: ‘We have heard’” and “He said: ‘I only call upon my Lord’” (1), and what follows it through the end of the sūrah, which they read with a kasrah, except for “so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord.”

Abū ʿAmr read all of them with a kasrah [from the beginning] through “if they had remained straight on the path”; he read that and what follows it with a fatḥah (4).
They therefore read them with a fatḥah because they are governed by “believed.”

The reading I prefer is a fatḥah where the passage is revelation and a kasrah where it is the words of the jinn, because this is the most eloquent Arabic and clearest in meaning, even though the other readings have defensible grounds.

x: Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of God, mighty and exalted:
h

And that our fool used to say outrageous things about God (4), and we had thought that humankind and jinn would never utter a lie about God (5). And men among humankind used to seek refuge in men among the jinn, so they increased them in burden (6).
Abū Jaʿfar, may God have mercy on him, says: God, mighty and exalted, reports the words of the group of jinn who listened to the Qurʾān: “And that our fool used to say”—meaning Iblīs
n
Some authorities on interpretation said much the same as we have said. We mention who said this.

c: Bishr related to us: Yazīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah,
m: concerning His saying, “And that our fool used to say outrageous things about God.” He said: It was Iblīs.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān, from a man of Mecca, from Mujāhid,
m: concerning “our fool said outrageous things about God.” He said: It was Iblīs. Then Sufyān said: I heard that when a man prostrates, Iblīs sits and weeps, saying: Woe to him! He was commanded to prostrate but disobeyed, so he has the Fire; the son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and did so, so he has the Garden (1).

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā told me: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, who said:
m: Qatādah recited, “And that our fool used to say outrageous things about God
n
, and we had thought that humankind and jinn would never utter a lie about God.” He said: By God, the fool among the jinn disobeyed Him just as [the fool among humankind] disobeyed Him
n
. As for outrageous speech, it is speech that transgresses the bounds
n
. The authorities on interpretation said much the same as we have said.

c: Yūnus told me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd said
m: concerning His saying, “And that our fool used to say outrageous things about God.” He said: Great injustice (4).

x: His saying, “and we had thought that humankind and jinn would never utter a lie about God”: He says: They said: We had supposed
n
that the descendants of Adam and the jinn would not speak falsely about God. “Thought” [in this passage]
n

means doubt. These jinn denied that they had known anyone would dare to lie about God, because before they heard the Qurʾān, Before they learned that God had declared the claims that He had a wife, a child, and other forms of disbelief to be false, they supposed that Iblīs was truthful in urging the descendants of Adam toward the various kinds of unbelief. When they heard the Qurʾān, they became certain that he had been lying about all of it. That is why they said: “Our fool used to say outrageous things about God.” They called him a fool.

His saying, “And that men among humankind used to seek refuge in men among the jinn”: God, exalted is His mention, reports the words of this group: Men among humankind used to seek protection from men among the jinn while traveling, whenever they camped at a place.
We have been told that this was their practice, as related to me by Muḥammad b. Saʿd:

c: My father related to me; my uncle related to me; my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning His saying, “And that men among humankind used to seek refuge in men among the jinn.” He said: In pre-Islamic times, when a man spent the night in a valley, he would say: I seek refuge with the mighty one of this valley
n
. This only increased their sin
n

c: Al-Ḥasan b. ʿArafah related to us: Hushaym related to us, from ʿAwf, from al-Ḥasan,
m: concerning the verse. He said: When one of them camped in a valley and spent the night there, he would say: I seek refuge with the mighty one of this valley from the foolish ones among his people
n

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Ibrāhīm,
m: [concerning His saying, “And that there were men”
n

among humankind who sought refuge in men among the jinn]. He said: When they camped in a valley, they would say: We seek refuge with the lord of this valley from whatever is in it. The jinn would reply: We have no power to harm or benefit you—or even ourselves.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Jarīr related to us, from Manṣūr, from Ibrāhīm,
m: concerning the same verse. He said: In pre-Islamic times, when people camped in a valley, they would say: We seek refuge with the lord of this valley [from whatever is in it]
n
. The jinn would say: You seek refuge in us, though we have no power to harm or benefit ourselves!
Muḥammad b. ʿAmr told me: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us: ʿĪsā related to us.

c: Al-Ḥārith also told me: al-Ḥasan related to us: Warqāʾ related to us,
m: both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, concerning “they sought refuge in men among the jinn.” He said: When they descended into a valley, they would say: We seek refuge with the great ones of this valley
n

c: Bishr related to us: Yazīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah,
m: concerning the verse. He said: We were told that this Arab tribe, whenever it camped in a valley, would say: We seek refuge with the mightiest one in this place. God says: “so they increased them in burden”—that is, in sin, and the jinn thereby became bolder toward them
n

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah,
m: concerning “they sought refuge in men among the jinn.” He said: In pre-Islamic times, when they camped somewhere, they would say: We seek refuge with the mightiest one in this place (4).

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Mihrān related to us, from Abū Jaʿfar, from al-Rabīʿ b.
m: Anas, concerning the verse. He said: They used to say: So-and-so among the jinn is the lord of this valley. When a man entered the valley, he sought refuge with its lord instead of God. He said: [That increased them]
n
in burden, which is fear
n

c: Yūnus told me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd said
m: concerning His saying, “And that men among humankind used to seek refuge in men among the jinn, so they increased them in burden.” He said: In pre-Islamic times, when a man camped in a valley, he would say: I seek refuge with the great one of this valley. When Islam came, they sought refuge with God and left them.

x: His saying, “so they increased them in burden”: The authorities on interpretation differed about its meaning.
Some said that it means the humans increased the jinn’s boldness toward them by seeking refuge in their mighty ones, and thereby they themselves increased in sin. We mention who said this.

c: Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: My father related to me; my uncle related to me; my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning “so they increased them in burden.” He said: That increased their sin
n

c: Bishr related to us: Yazīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah, who said:
m: God said, “so they increased them in burden”—that is, in sin, and the jinn became bolder toward them.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah,
m: concerning “so they increased them in burden.” He says: In transgression
n

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Ibrāhīm,
m: concerning the same verse. He said: They became bolder toward them
n

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Jarīr related to us, from Manṣūr, from Ibrāhīm,
m: with the same wording.

x: Others said that what is meant is that the unbelievers increased in their transgression
n
. We mention who said this.

m: Muḥammad b. ʿAmr told me: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us: ʿĪsā related to us.

c: Al-Ḥārith also told me: al-Ḥasan related to us: Warqāʾ related to us,
m: both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, concerning the verse. He said: The unbelievers increased in transgression
n

x: Others said that it means: They increased them in fear. We mention who said this.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Mihrān related to us, from Abū Jaʿfar, from al-Rabīʿ b.
m: Anas, concerning the verse. He said: This increased their fear
n

c: Yūnus told me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd said
m: concerning His saying, “so they increased them in burden.” He said: The jinn increased their fear
n

. In our view, the soundest interpretation is that the humans increased the jinn in sin by what they did, because they thereby encouraged them to regard God’s forbidden things as permissible. In Arabic, rahq means sin and committing forbidden acts. Al-Aʿshā said
n
: “Nothing benefits me apart from seeing her; can a lover
n
find relief if he does not commit a forbidden act?” That is, unless he commits something forbidden.

x: Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of God, mighty and exalted:
h
And they thought, as you thought, that God would never raise anyone (7). And we probed the sky, and found it filled with stern guards and shooting stars (8).
Abū Jaʿfar says: God, exalted is His mention, reports these jinn as saying, “And they thought, as you thought, that God would never raise anyone (7).”

He means that the jinn men supposed, as human men supposed, that God would never raise a messenger among His creatures to call them to affirm His oneness. The authorities on interpretation said much the same as we have said.

c: Bishr related to us: Yazīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from al-Kalbī,
m: concerning the verse: “The unbelieving jinn thought, as the unbelieving humans thought, that God would never send a messenger”
n

x: His saying, “And we probed the sky”: God, mighty and exalted, reports this group as saying: We sought the sky and its regions
n
, “and found it filled”—we found it had been filled
n
—“with stern guards,” meaning guardians
n
, “and shooting stars.” These are the plural of shihāb, the stars used to pelt the devils. The authorities on interpretation said much the same as we have said. We mention who said this.

x: Discussion of the interpretation of His saying: {And among us are Muslims, and among us are the unjust. Whoever submits—
those have sought right guidance (14). But as for the unjust, they will be firewood for Hell” (15).} “They have sought right guidance. As for those who act unjustly, they will be fuel for Hell.”
God reports the jinn saying, “Among us are those who submit,” humbling themselves before God in obedience, “and among us are those who deviate,” turning away from Islam and the right path.

The interpreters said similarly. Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related from his father, from his uncle, from his father, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that “those who deviate” are those who turn from the truth. Mujāhid said they are wrongdoers. Qatādah said they are unjust. Ibn Zayd said the muqsiṭ is just, while the qāsiṭ is unjust. Ibn Zayd cited poetry about acting unjustly toward kings in the time of Tubbaʿ, and compared qāsiṭ and muqsiṭ to turāb and mutrib: turāb is a poor person, as in “or a destitute person covered in dust” [Qur’an 90:16], while mutrib is wealthy.

Regarding “Whoever submits, those have sought right guidance,” he says: whoever submits to God and obeys Him has deliberately pursued right guidance in religion. “Those who deviate” are those who turn away from Islam; they will be fuel with which Hell is kindled.

Interpretation of God’s words: “If they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink, so that We might test them with it. Whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will lead him into an escalating punishment” (72:16–17).
had these deviants remained on the path of truth, We would have expanded their provision and worldly means. “So that We might test them with it” means to put them to trial through it.

The interpreters differed. Some agreed with this explanation. Ibn ʿAbbās said that remaining upright means obedience, abundant water means pure water in great quantity, and testing them means trying them through it. Mujāhid said the path is Islam; abundant water is plentiful beneficial provision, and the test is that they return to their decreed wretchedness. Reports from Mujāhid through Sufyān give the same explanation; one says it is the path of truth and that they are tested until they return to their decreed wretchedness. Mujāhid said the path is Islam, abundant water is plentiful, and testing means trying them. He also explained abundant water as wealth, and the test as their return to what God knows of them. Mujāhid further said that “We would have given them abundant water” means “We would have given them much wealth.”

Regarding “so that We might test them with it,” he said: so that We might try them. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said the path is religion, abundant water means much wealth, and the test is trying them through it. Qatādah was asked about “If they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink.” He said: had they all believed, God would have broadened their worldly provision, in order to test them. Qatādah also said that if they believed their provision would be expanded, and that the test is through it. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas explained abundant water as a comfortable life. Ibn Zayd said it means plentiful water, and testing them means trying them. Al-Suddī related that ʿUmar said: “Wherever there is water, there is wealth; and wherever there is wealth, there is a trial.”
Others said the meaning is: if they remained in misguidance, We would grant them ample provision to draw them gradually toward ruin. Abū Mijlaz said it means remaining on the path of misguidance.
Others said it means that if they remained on the path of truth and believed, God would expand their provision. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said this is like God’s words,
“Had they upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to them from their Lord, they would have had provision from above them and beneath their feet”
and
“Had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened for them blessings from heaven and earth”
Abundant water means abundant wealth; testing them means trying them through it.

Regarding “Whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will lead him into an escalating punishment,” God means whoever turns away from the reminder his Lord has given him, namely this Qur’an. In other words, whoever turns away from listening to the Qur’an and acting upon it, God will lead into “an escalating punishment,” meaning a severe, arduous punishment.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as a stretch of punishment through which one climbs. Mujāhid said it is a hardship of punishment. ʿIkrimah, reporting from Ibn ʿAbbās, said it is a mountain in Hell. Qatādah said it is punishment without respite. Qatādah also explained it as ascending punishment from God, with no relief. Ibn Zayd said ṣaʿad is exhausting punishment. The reciters differed over the reading of “yaslukhu” (“He leads him”): some reciters of Mecca and Basra read “naslukhu” (“We lead him”), taking the first-person form from the wording “so that We might test them with it.” Most reciters of Kufa read it with the yāʾ, “yaslukhu,” meaning “God leads him,” referring back to “his Lord.”

x: Interpretation of His words: “The mosques belong to God, so do not call upon anyone alongside God. When God’s servant stood calling upon Him, they nearly crowded around him in dense groups” (72:18–19).

God Most High says to His Prophet Muḥammad: “Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened,” and it has also been revealed to me that “the mosques belong to God, so do not call upon anyone alongside God.” People, do not associate anything with Him there; rather, affirm His oneness alone and devote worship sincerely to Him.

The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said that when Jews and Christians entered their churches and synagogues, they associated partners with God, so God commanded His Prophet to worship God alone. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr related that the jinn said to God’s Prophet: “How can we come to the mosque when we are far from you? How can we attend the prayer with you?” Then this verse was revealed: “The mosques belong to God, so do not call upon anyone alongside God.” Qatādah also said that God commanded His Prophet to direct supplication sincerely to Him when entering the mosque. ʿIkrimah said “the mosques” means all mosques. Regarding “When God’s servant stood calling upon Him, they nearly crowded around him in dense groups”: He means Muḥammad, God’s Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, calling upon God—that is, saying “There is no god but God.” They nearly formed crowds upon Muḥammad, one group piled over another.

The singular is libdah, with two pronunciations: libdah, with kasrah, whose plural is libad; and lubdah, with ḍammah, whose plural is lubad. There is also lābid, whose plural is lubbad, like rākʿ and rukkaʿ. The regional reciters read libad with kasrah, except Ibn Muḥayṣin, who used ḍammah; the two have the same meaning, though I prefer the reading followed by the regional reciters. In Arabic, a mass of locusts piled atop one another is called a libdah. ʿAbd Manāf ibn Ribʿ al-Hudhalī said: “They struck with six houses and four, until they seemed to have upon them a swarm of locusts.” A jābī is a locust that gathers and eats everything.
The interpreters differed about who is meant by “they nearly crowded around him in dense groups.”

evidence.text: The regional reciters read libad with kasrah, except Ibn Muḥayṣin, who used ḍammah; the two have the same meaning, though I prefer the reading followed by the regional reciters.

x: Some said the jinn nearly crowded upon God’s Messenger when they heard the Qur’an. Ibn ʿAbbās said that when they heard the Prophet reciting, they nearly clambered over one another out of eagerness to hear him and came close, though he did not know they were there, until the Messenger came to him and recited: “Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened.” Al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise said they nearly climbed over him in eagerness for the Qur’an they heard. Abū Jaʿfar said those who hold this view take “When God’s servant stood calling upon Him” as part of what was revealed to the Prophet, so the meaning is: “Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened, and that when God’s servant stood calling upon Him…” Others said these words are the jinn’s report to their people when they returned, telling them what they had seen of the Prophet’s Companions obeying him and following his lead in bowing and prostration.

Those who said this include: Muḥammad ibn Maʿmar related from Abū Hishām, from Abū ʿAwānah, from Abū Bishr, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said this was the jinn speaking to their people: “When God’s servant stood calling upon Him, they nearly crowded around him.” They saw him praying while his Companions bowed and prostrated as he did, and were amazed at their obedience to him. Jarīr related from Mughīrah, from Ziyād, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, that the Prophet’s Companions followed him in prayer, bowing and prostrating as he did. Those who hold the view reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd read the initial hamzah in “wa-annahu” with fatḥah, linking it to “and that the majesty of our Lord is exalted”; it may also be read with kasrah as a new sentence.

Others said this is God’s own report revealed to His Prophet: God knew that humans and jinn had joined forces against him to extinguish the truth he brought, but God insisted on bringing it to completion. Qatādah said: “The jinn and humans joined forces against this cause to extinguish it, but God refused except to support it, bring it to completion, and make it prevail over those who opposed it.” Qatādah also said that when the Prophet stood, jinn and humans banded together, striving to extinguish the light God had sent down. Ibn Zayd said they supported one another against God’s Messenger. Those who hold this view read the initial hamzah in “wa-annahu” with fatḥah. In our view, the soundest interpretation is that God reports how, when His Messenger Muḥammad stood calling upon Him, the Arabs nearly united against him to extinguish God’s light. We prefer this because “When God’s servant stood calling upon Him” follows “The mosques belong to God,” which is a report from God; this clause is likewise a report.

Also, it follows “so do not call upon anyone alongside God,” so what follows naturally reports what the one commanded not to call upon anyone faced—not how quickly those being called responded. Muḥammad ibn Bashshār related from Hawdhah, from ʿAwf, from al-Ḥasan, regarding “When God’s servant stood calling upon Him”: when God’s Messenger stood saying “There is no god but God” and calling people to their Lord, the Arabs nearly all rallied against him. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said “they nearly crowded around him” means they piled upon him. Another report from Saʿīd says they were one upon another. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as “supporters.”

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā, and al-Ḥārith related to me
m: … What follows is a report of what the one commanded not to call upon anyone alongside God faced, not about the number or speed of those called upon responding. Al-Ḥasan said that when God’s Messenger stood saying “There is no god but God” and calling people to their Lord, the Arabs nearly all rallied against him. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said they piled upon him, one over another. Ibn ʿAbbās explained “they nearly crowded around him” as “supporters.”

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā, and al-Ḥārith related to me
m: … from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ, both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said “they would be upon him in dense groups” means all together. Ibn Zayd likewise said they were all together; lubad means something piled one thing upon another.

evidence.text: Those who hold the view reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd read the initial hamzah in “wa-annahu” with fatḥah, linking it to “and that the majesty of our Lord is exalted”; it may also be read with kasrah as a new sentence.

x: Interpretation of His words: “Say: I call only upon my Lord and associate no one with Him. Say: I have no power to harm you or guide you. Say: No one can protect me from God, nor will I find any refuge apart from Him” (72:20–22). Abū Jaʿfar said the reciters differed over “qul innamā adʿū rabbī.” Most reciters of Medina and Basra and some of Kufa read it as a statement, “He said,” making it God’s report that His Prophet Muḥammad said: “When God’s servant stood calling upon Him, they crowded around him; he said to them: I call only upon my Lord and associate no one with Him.” Some Medinese reciters and most of Kufa read it as God’s command to His Prophet… …Muḥammad: “Say, Muḥammad, to the people who nearly crowded around you: I call only upon my Lord and associate no one with Him.” In my view, both are established readings, and whichever one a reciter uses is correct.

evidence.text: Abū Jaʿfar said the reciters differed over “qul innamā adʿū rabbī.”

Most reciters of Medina and Basra and some of Kufa read it as a statement, “He said,” making it God’s report that His Prophet Muḥammad said: “When God’s servant stood calling upon Him, they crowded around him; he said to them: I call only upon my Lord and associate no one with Him.”

Some Medinese reciters and most of Kufa read it as God’s command to His Prophet… …Muḥammad: “Say, Muḥammad, to the people who nearly crowded around you: I call only upon my Lord and associate no one with Him.”

x: Regarding “Say: I have no power to harm you or guide you,” God tells His Prophet Muḥammad to say to the Arab polytheists who rejected his counsel: “I have no power over harm to you in your religion or worldly life, nor can I guide you to right guidance; the One who controls that is God, who holds dominion over everything.”

Regarding “Say: No one can protect me from God”: Say to them, no one among His creation can shield me from God if He wills something for me, nor can any helper aid me against Him. It is related that this verse was revealed because one of the jinn said, “I will protect him.” Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related from al-Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān, from his father, that Ḥaḍramī claimed it had been mentioned to him that a notable jinn with a following said: “Muḥammad only wants us to protect him, and I will protect him.” So God revealed: “Say: No one can protect me from God.”

Regarding “nor will I find any refuge apart from Him”: I will find no shelter to which I can flee apart from God. Qatādah explained it as “a refuge and a helper”; another report from Qatādah says “a shelter,” while Sufyān said “a supporter.”

Interpretation of His words: “It is only a proclamation from God and His messages. Whoever disobeys God and His Messenger will have the Fire of Hell, remaining there forever. When they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in support and fewer in number” (72:23–24).

God tells His Prophet Muḥammad to say to the Arab polytheists: “I have no power to harm you or guide you”—“except to deliver a proclamation from God and His messages.” That is, I can only convey what God commanded me to deliver and the messages with which He sent me. Guidance and abandonment are in God’s hand alone; He guides whom He wills and abandons whom He wills. Qatādah said: “That is what I control: conveying from God and His messages.” Another possible interpretation is that “illā” is two separate particles, with “lā” disconnected from “in”; the meaning would then be: “Say: no one can protect me from God if I fail to convey His messages.” “Conveying” would be in the accusative because an apodosis verb is understood, as in “if not giving, then a gracious refusal,” meaning “if you do not give, then refuse graciously.”

Regarding “Whoever disobeys God and His Messenger will have the Fire of Hell”: God says that whoever disobeys Him in what He commands and forbids, rejects His Messenger, and denies his message will enter the Fire of Hell. “Remaining there forever” means staying there without end.

Regarding “until they see what they are promised”: until they witness the punishment their Lord promised them and the coming of the Hour, then they will know who is weaker in support and fewer in number: God’s forces, which they associated as partners, or these polytheists?

Interpretation of His words: “Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set a distant term for it. He is Knower of the unseen, and He reveals His unseen to no one, except to a messenger He has chosen; then He sends guards before him and behind him” (72:25–27).

God tells His Prophet Muḥammad to say to the polytheists among his people: I do not know whether the punishment and the coming of the Hour your Lord promises you are near, or whether my Lord has appointed a known term far off.

Regarding “Knower of the unseen, and He reveals His unseen to no one, except to a messenger He has chosen”: God, mighty and exalted, means that He knows what is hidden from His creation’s sight. He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, informing or showing it to them, except a messenger He has chosen; He reveals of it whatever He wills.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās said God informed the messengers of revelation from the unseen and disclosed it to them through what He revealed; what God decrees is known to no one but Him. Qatādah said God selects the messengers and informs them of whatever unseen matters He wills. Another report from Qatādah says He reveals of the unseen whatever He wills to a messenger when He is pleased with him. Ibn Zayd said God sends down from His unseen whatever He wills to the prophets; He sent down the Qur’an, which is unseen, to God’s Messenger, and informed us in it of unseen events that will occur on the Day of Resurrection.
Regarding “then He sends guards before him and behind him”: He sends guardians and protectors in front of and behind the messenger to guard him.
The interpreters said the same.

Among those who said this: al-Ḍaḥḥāk said that when an angel was sent to the Prophet with revelation, other angels were sent with him to guard him in front and behind, so Satan could not appear in the angel’s form. Ibrāhīm said they are angels guarding them in front and behind. Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif, reporting from Ibrāhīm, said the angels guard him from the jinn. Another report from Ibrāhīm says they guard him from the jinn in front and behind. Ibn ʿAbbās said these are successive angels guarding the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, from Satan until what he was sent with becomes clear to them; this is when God says, “so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord.” Qatādah said they are guards among the angels.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord, while He encompasses all that is with them and keeps count of everything” (72:28).
The interpreters differed over who is meant by “so that He may know.”

Some said it means God’s Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: so that the Messenger of God may know that the messengers before him conveyed their Lord’s messages. Qatādah said that the Prophet may know that the messengers before him conveyed what came from their Lord and preserved it. Another report from Qatādah says the Prophet of God may know that the messengers conveyed from God and that God protected them.

Others said it means that the polytheists may know that the messengers conveyed their Lord’s messages. Mujāhid said it is so that those who denied the messengers may know that they conveyed their Lord’s messages.

Others said it means that Muḥammad may know that the angels conveyed the messages of their Lord. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said that four guardian angels accompany Gabriel. Muḥammad then knows “that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord, while He encompasses all that is with them and keeps count of everything.” Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said that whenever Gabriel descended with revelation, four guardian angels accompanied him. In our view, the soundest of these interpretations is that the Messenger may know that the messengers before him conveyed their Lord’s messages. “So that he may know” is connected to “He sends guards before him and behind him,” which is a report about the Messenger; therefore “so that he may know” is connected to that report.
Regarding “He encompasses all that is with them”: He knows everything they possess. “He keeps count of everything” means He knows the number of all things, and nothing is hidden from Him.

c: Muḥammad ibn Bashshār related to us from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar, from Shuʿbah, from Abū Bishr, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said
m: about this verse, from “except a messenger He has chosen” through “He keeps count of everything”: “So that the messengers know their Lord encompasses them and they may convey their Lord’s messages.” This concludes the commentary on Sūrat al-Jinn.
